newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's MCI mix risky when no inflation pressure -BT.
newsitem.headline: NZ's MCI mix risky when no inflation pressure -BT.

text.p: The structure of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's Monetary Conditions Index (MCI) threatens to be self-defeating in its aim to help battle inflation when the currency moves sharply, Bankers Trust (BT) economists said.
Their comments chimed with a widespread tone of discomfort being expressed around the New Zealand money market this week as a slide in the dollar has forced up wholesale interest rates.
Markets are forced to push up the 90-day bank bill rate to keep the RBNZ's MCI within its desired range and hold monetary conditions at a level the central bank says is acceptable.
The jumps in bill rates which have resulted from the latest falls in the dollar have prompted many to question the effectiveness of the MCI as policy management tool.

In a report entitled "Not all MCIs are equal - The mix does matter", BT economists David Plank and Nick Bennenbroek observed that the RBNZ's preset trade-off between the currency's Trade Weighted Index(TWI) and 90-day bill rates that underpins the MCI is too inflexible to be able to suit all states of the economy.

"The impact of interest rates and the exchange rate on inflation will vary over time with the stage of the business cycle. Levels, as well as rates of change, also matter at some point," the pair said.
At present, there is widespread acceptance that New Zealand is in a period of very low inflationary pressure that is coinciding with a slowdown and trough in economic growth.
"With inflationary pressures non-existent in the tradable sector and domestic demand weak, the threat from the falling TWI is minimal," the BT economists said.
Mortgage rates have trended downwards in recent months, tracking a clear movement downwards in rates and yields on virtually all maturities across the debt market curve since late last year.

Yet, because of the MCI's mechanism, the drop in the kiwi dollar -- which has lost three cents against the U.S. dollar in three weeks -- a sharp upward move has been forced in short-dated bill rates, to the point where lenders say they will have to raise mortgage rates or risk financial loss.

"In the present economic environment, we would assess the deflationary impact of significantly higher interest rates as being greater than the inflationary impact for an equivalent fall in the exchange rate," Plank and Bennenbroek added.

"With the market already pricing in a large fall in short-term interest rates, this should be able to take place without putting too much pressure on the currency, unless the economy suffers a harder landing than currently expected," they warned.
By 2.00 p.m. (0200 GMT) on Friday the New Zealand dollar was steady at 0.6500/07 -- exactly one U.S. cent below its Thursday close -- and the TWI stood at 64.61 about half a point down.
At the same time the MCI level was steady at just under 773, about 52 basis points, as expressed in interest rate terms, easier than the RBNZ's current target level of 825.
To maintain that level of MCI 90-day bill rates stood at 8.52 percent, up 82 basis points from Thursday's 7.70 percent close.
Yet the 825 target level set by the RBNZ for the September quarter was based on a desire for a TWI of 67.3 and interest rates of 7.00 percent, the BT economists noted.

With current rates apparently 150 basis points tighter than this, and the currency several percentage points weaker, BT said the trade-off link seemed to be causing an overstatement of how much conditions have eased.
